passage: Anand said yes to everything that carried the director's name: the launch deck, the town-hall demo, the client dashboard, the hackathon team. In his Mumbai office his calendar looked like a bus timetable. By week six he had missed the deadline on the dashboard, and then the next one, on a quarterly report. Samir, across from him at lunch, said gently, "You're on eleven things." Anand shrugged. "Visibility matters." At the review, his manager laid the list on the table: eleven activities, two late, none finished with real depth. "It looks scattered," the manager said. Anand went home wondering whether being seen and being trusted with a big goal were really the same thing.

qa.q: How many things was Anand working on?
qa.a: Anand was working on eleven things.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Samir mentioned the eleven things?
qa.a: Anand felt defensive, shrugging it off by saying visibility matters, before the review left him unsettled.

qa.q: What could Anand do instead of taking every high-profile task, and why?
qa.a: Anand could choose two or three tasks that matter most and finish them well, because a few clear results make a stronger record than many half-done ones.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt watching Anand's schedule fill up?
qa.a: Samir was probably concerned for Anand, which is why Samir raised it gently over lunch.

grounding: Illustrates taking on every high-profile task, spreading thin and missing deadlines, so the many activities look scattered rather than strong.
